summary: Created a LUKS2-encrypted volume on node1 (RHEL7) backed by a 2G loopback image, auto-unlocked via a root-only keyfile, and mounted at /srv/secure automatically at boot. Verified end-to-end across an actual node restart: boot_id changed, secure-loop.service attached the loop device, systemd-cryptsetup@secure.service unlocked the LUKS volume, and /srv/secure was mounted with prior data intact - all without any manual intervention.
actions_performed: Discovered node1 had no free disk/LVM space; provisioned a 2G file-backed loop device instead (/var/lib/secure-vol/secure.img, loop10)
cryptsetup package was unavailable (no subscription-manager repos); added a temporary CentOS-7 vault HTTP repo and installed cryptsetup 2.0.3
Generated a 2048-bit root-only keyfile (/etc/luks/secure.key, mode 400) and luksFormat'd the loop device as LUKS2
Created an xfs filesystem on the mapped device, mounted at /srv/secure, wrote a test marker file
Added systemd oneshot unit secure-loop.service (Before=systemd-cryptsetup@secure.service/cryptsetup.target) to reattach the loop device at boot before cryptsetup runs
Added /etc/crypttab entry (secure /dev/loop10 /etc/luks/secure.key luks) and /etc/fstab entry (/dev/mapper/secure /srv/secure xfs defaults 0 2)
Enabled secure-loop.service, daemon-reloaded, and live-tested the full chain (loop attach -> LUKS unlock -> mount) without reboot
Captured pre-restart baseline (boot_id, mount state, crypt status, marker file) on node1
Triggered a safe self-scheduled reboot (systemd-run --on-active=1 systemctl reboot) so acknowledgement returned before disconnection
Polled node1 until exec access returned and confirmed boot_id changed (33b0e84c... -> 5bf15ff6...), proving an actual restart occurred

Verified post-restart: secure-loop.service and systemd-cryptsetup@secure.service both active since boot, loop10 attached, /dev/mapper/secure active LUKS2 device, /srv/secure mounted xfs rw, pre-reboot marker file intact, and a new post-reboot write succeeded

evidence.requirement: Healthy baseline before restart (boot identity, mount, crypt status)
evidence.summary: Captured boot_id 33b0e84c-4dd1-406a-8f89-2e8ceca97bd6, active LUKS mapping, /srv/secure mounted rw, and marker.txt content prior to restart.

evidence.requirement: Encrypted volume created and functional (LUKS format, filesystem, mount, data)
evidence.summary: Backing file created, keyfile generated, loop10 attached, luksFormat succeeded (LUKS2), xfs filesystem created, mounted at /srv/secure, marker file written and read back, cleanly unmounted/closed.

evidence.requirement: Auto-unlock/auto-mount configuration installed (crypttab, fstab, systemd unit)
evidence.summary: secure-loop.service enabled and Before=cryptsetup ordering configured; /etc/crypttab and /etc/fstab entries added; live simulation of the boot chain (loop attach -> cryptsetup attach -> mount -a) succeeded and marker.txt was readable.
systemd-run scheduled a deferred reboot so the exec call returned 'reboot scheduled' immediately, before the node went down.

evidence.requirement: Node restart actually occurred (changed boot identity)
evidence.summary: Node became unreachable (connection timed out) confirming shutdown in progress, then came back with a new boot_id 5bf15ff6-4404-4477-bc54-be56077dce00, distinct from the pre-restart 33b0e84c..., proving a genuine reboot.

evidence.requirement: Post-restart recovery: encrypted volume auto-unlocked and auto-mounted without manual action, data intact
evidence.summary: After reboot, secure-loop.service and systemd-cryptsetup@secure.service both show Active since the boot timestamp with no manual intervention; /dev/mapper/secure is an active LUKS2 device; /srv/secure is mounted xfs rw; pre-reboot marker.txt content survived and a new post-reboot write succeeded, confirming full read/write functionality.

evidence.requirement: Configuration persistence (crypttab, fstab, enabled unit, key/file permissions)
evidence.summary: Confirmed /etc/crypttab and /etc/fstab entries persisted post-reboot, secure-loop.service is enabled, and the keyfile/backing image retain root-only permissions (400/600).
